title: GitLab Secrets Manager: Govern secrets like your code
summary:
Credentials often start in an engineer's local dev environments, then get copied into unscoped CI/CD variables to keep pipelines running. Stored there as a raw value rather than a reference to a scoped secret, a signing key reaches every job in the pipeline — compromised or not.

Standing up a standalone vault narrows that exposure but requires mirroring every change to project membership, protected branches, and production environments. When the vault falls out of sync, a pipeline breaks or an agent’s service account keeps access it no longer needs.

GitLab Secrets Manager tightens credential security without a second permission model. It is now generally available in GitLab 19.5 for Premium and Ultimate on GitLab.com and GitLab Self-Managed, with GitLab Dedicated coming soon. Built on OpenBao, it stores build-time and runtime credentials under the same permissions and audit trail as your code. Platform teams can offer developers self-service secrets, and security teams get credentials scoped to the jobs that use them, plus the pipeline and job ID on every CI/CD read.

"GitLab Secrets Manager lets us centralize secrets across CI/CD, Kubernetes, and infrastructure as code without standing up multiple vaults or maintaining separate integration points. It also strengthens our supply chain security by tightening which users and pipelines can access a given credential." - Jeremy Nauta, Software Architect, OneTrust

How Secrets Manager scopes build-time secrets to each job

Agents can take actions no one anticipated, so security teams need to regard every job as if its agents will use any credential it can reach. Secrets Manager narrows what agents can reach with the context GitLab already holds about each job: its project, the branch it runs on, whether that branch is protected, and the environment it targets.

A developer declares the secret a job needs with the secrets: keyword in .gitlab-ci.yml, and GitLab injects the value only into jobs that declare it and fall within its scope. Scope conditions accept wildcards on branch and environment, and they combine, so one rule can require a protected branch and a production/* environment before a job receives the credential.

Inside the job, GitLab writes the value to a temporary file and exposes only its path, which limits exposure in subprocesses, crash dumps, and telemetry. GitLab masks the value in job logs and discards it when the job ends. Unlike a CI/CD variable, a secret is never readable in your project configuration. OpenBao encrypts secrets at rest with AES-256-GCM, so a copy of the secrets database holds only ciphertext. Jobs fetch values straight from OpenBao with short-lived tokens bound to each job’s identity, which keeps plaintext secrets out of the GitLab application.

Revoke and trace an exposed credential

When the axios npm package was compromised, a SANS advisory warned teams to "assume all environment variables on affected systems were exfiltrated" and extend investigations to CI/CD runners and build infrastructure. Responders had to work out which credentials each affected job could read, how to cut off access, and which runs read them.

With Secrets Manager, when a job runs a poisoned dependency, the exposure stops at the secrets that job declared and was authorized to read. To clean up, revoke and replace the leaked credential, update the value in Secrets Manager, and audit that one job while other pipelines keep running. Secrets Manager prompts you to set a rotation reminder when you create a secret. Dynamic credentials are coming soon and will provide ephemeral access without manual rotation.

GitLab streams every secret create, read, update, and delete event to your audit event destinations and records changes in the audit trail. Each pipeline read carries the pipeline and job IDs, which tie to the commit, the triggering user, and the merge request, when there is one. Incident responders and auditors can trace a read to the change behind it without correlating logs from a CI system, a vault, and an identity provider. Audit events never contain secret values.

Govern secrets with the permissions that govern your code

As agents take on more work, platform teams field more requests for pipelines and service accounts that need credentials. When those requests queue, teams fall back on broad grants and shared secrets.

Secrets Manager uses the GitLab namespace as its isolation boundary. Projects inherit secrets defined in the groups above them, so you define a shared credential once. Owners grant read, write, and delete permissions to specific users or default roles, using the same membership model that governs the code. Remove a person or an agent's service account from a project, and that identity's access to the project's secrets ends.

Developers reference secrets through the project access they already hold. When a secret reference breaks, they fix it in the same merge request as the code, with no second repository, approver, or access ticket. With a governed credential one line away, fewer secrets end up in over-scoped CI/CD variables, local files, or the repository.

One store for pipelines and runtime workloads

Kubernetes, Terraform, and scripts often get separate secret stores, each with its own access model and logs. Secrets Manager serves runtime tools from the same store as pipelines, under the same permissions and audit trail:

  • Kubernetes, through External Secrets Operator. ESO re-fetches the secret on a set interval and updates the Kubernetes Secret in place, so a rotated value reaches the cluster without a pipeline run.
  • Terraform and OpenTofu. They read a secret as a data source at plan or apply time and keep credentials out of .tfvars files and CI/CD variables.
  • OpenBao and Vault CLIs, through the Vault-compatible API. Teams keep their existing scripts and point them at Secrets Manager.
  • Other runtime tools, through the Secrets Manager API.

Each runtime tool authenticates with a service account or an access token, and that identity needs project membership and explicit read permission for the secret. GitLab then issues a separate token, valid for five minutes, that the tool uses to fetch it.

How Secrets Manager fits with GitLab's supply chain controls

GitLab’s governed software factory connects code, pipelines, packages, and secrets on one platform, with one identity model and one record of how a change reached production. Dependency Firewall decides which packages enter a pipeline, Secrets Manager limits which credentials the pipeline can reach, and Artifact Central governs what you ship.

Secrets Manager supports two of the five stages in the GitLab Security Standard, GitLab's framework for letting agents earn autonomy: For Authorize, it binds each job to the secrets its identity and scope allow, and for Respond, it streams every CRUD event.

Secret push protection blocks commits containing credentials before they reach the repository, and Secret detection finds the ones already in your code and history. GitLab Duo Agent Platform triages what those scans find and flags likely false positives, so your team revokes, rotates, and audits only real leaks.

GitLab's existing integrations for HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, and Google Cloud Secret Manager keep working alongside Secrets Manager, so you can migrate at your own pace.

Get started

GitLab Secrets Manager is a paid add-on for Premium and Ultimate, billed through GitLab Credits: 1 credit per secret stored per month, and 1 credit per 2,500 read operations. An enterprise license agreement is available for air-gapped environments.

  • On GitLab.com, top-level group Owners can try GitLab Secrets Manager free for 30 days or 500 evaluation credits, whichever ends first. Go to your top-level group, select Secure > Secrets Manager, then Start 30-day trial.
  • On GitLab Self-Managed, your administrator must install and enable Secrets Manager, following the documented sizing and high-availability guidance.
  • GitLab Dedicated support is coming soon.

To find the first credentials to move, run the secret audit tool for CI/CD variables, which flags variables likely to hold credentials. A migration workflow for CI/CD variables is in development.

Have suggestions or feedback? Share them in the Secrets Manager feedback issue.

title: Get every merge request in front of the right reviewer, faster
summary:
The code is written. Now who reviews it?

The volume of code has never been greater, but delivery hasn’t kept pace. At Meta, code changes on internal platforms grew 220% year over year, while changes that reached users as new features grew only 36% (Reuters, August 2026). Every one of those changes has to clear review before it reaches users.

Automated review absorbs much of that load. Code Review Flow in GitLab Duo Agent Platform reviews merge requests as they arrive, follows custom review instructions you define per project, and costs a flat 0.25 GitLab Credits per review ($0.25 at list price). If a manual review takes about 15 minutes of a senior engineer’s time, that’s roughly $25 per review, so automated review cuts per-review cost by 99% (GitLab).

Automated review doesn’t take people out of the loop. Approval rules, CODEOWNERS, and compliance policies still require a person to sign off on many changes. For those merge requests, the first slowdown is often finding the right reviewer, and it happens before anyone reads a line. The right reviewer needs expertise in the code being changed, room in their queue, and availability in a time zone where they can respond quickly. When authors can’t see those factors, a few senior engineers carry most of the reviews while other qualified reviewers sit idle.

GitLab 19.5 removes that step with Recommend Reviewers Flow. When you create a merge request, GitLab recommends the best individual reviewer based on workload, time zone, availability, and expertise defined by approval rules and CODEOWNERS. The flow explains why it chose that reviewer and lets you assign them in one click. Across your engineering organization, reviews start sooner, review load spreads across every qualified engineer, and more of the code your team writes reaches users.

Watch Recommend Reviewers Flow in action:

Review is a routing problem, not a headcount problem

Teams often treat slow reviews as a people problem. They add reminders, review rotations, extended time zone coverage, and escalations. Those workarounds cost people time and can lead to burnout, and they leave the real cause untouched: routing. The expertise and capacity already exist; there’s just nothing to match them to each merge request as it arrives.

Without that match, the author has to answer questions GitLab already can. Who knows this part of the codebase? Who has room in their queue? Who is online right now? Authors fall back on habits that slow everyone down:

  • Assigning a whole group. Everyone gets notified, nobody feels responsible, and the merge request waits for a volunteer.
  • Defaulting to the same trusted reviewer. That person becomes a bottleneck, and their own work stalls.
  • Guessing across time zones. The reviewer you picked just signed off for the day, so your feedback arrives tomorrow.

Reviewers pay a price, too. Group assignments flood their notifications with merge requests they will never review, which makes the ones that need them easier to miss. And the reviewers everyone defaults to absorb a growing share of the queue on top of their own work, which wears them down faster.

How intelligent reviewer suggestions work

GitLab Duo Agent Platform runs Recommend Reviewers Flow on your merge request and does the research for you:

  1. You create your merge request. A trigger starts the flow automatically when a merge request is created, whether in draft or ready state, so suggestions arrive from the start.
  2. The flow evaluates eligible reviewers. It weighs each candidate’s workload, time zone, availability, and expertise as defined by approval rules and CODEOWNERS, to find the person best suited and positioned to respond.
  3. You see the recommendation and the reasoning. The flow explains why it chose each reviewer, so you can approve the suggestion based on that context.
  4. You assign with one click. Suggestions appear in a dedicated panel on the merge request. You decide who reviews and when.

This design keeps you in control of timing. You can finish iterating or address automated code review feedback first, then bring in a human reviewer when the change is truly ready. You set it up as a flow trigger in your project rather than a project setting, so it fits alongside the other agentic workflows your team already runs.

What your team gains

The right reviewer match means faster feedback, clearer accountability, and a more balanced workload. Recommend Reviewers Flow makes that call consistently, at scale, and with reasoning you can see and override.

Recommend Reviewers Flow also works alongside the other foundational flows in GitLab Duo Agent Platform that handle the work around a merge request:

  • Run Code Review Flow first, so automated feedback lands before a person is brought in.
  • Add Security Review Flow to check merge request changes for business logic vulnerabilities before they merge.
  • Use Fix CI/CD Pipeline Flow to diagnose and repair failed jobs, so a broken pipeline doesn’t hold up an approved change.
  • Use Custom Flows to build Recommend Reviewers Flow into the process your team already follows.

Each step from merge request to merge runs on the same platform, under the same policies, so more of the code your team writes actually reaches users.

Get started

Intelligent reviewer suggestions are generally available in GitLab 19.5 for GitLab.com, GitLab Self-Managed, and GitLab Dedicated. To try them, add the Recommend Reviewers Flow trigger to your project, then create your next merge request. Learn more in our documentation.

New to GitLab Duo Agent Platform? Start a free trial today. Already a GitLab Premium or Ultimate subscriber? Turn on Duo Agent Platform and use the GitLab Credits included with your subscription.

title: Connect your agents to your software lifecycle with the GitLab MCP server
summary:
Agents are working across your team's software development lifecycle, but most still operate as separate tools, leaving the context, handoffs, and permissions for your team to stitch together. When your agents use APIs for these disparate tools, they often guess at endpoints and use up their context window on extra calls. The GitLab MCP server, now generally available with GitLab 19.5, connects your team’s external agents to your entire software lifecycle — from planning through production.

The GitLab MCP server enables any MCP-compatible agent to run GitLab workflows from the client your team already works in, getting what it needs in fewer calls and with less context bloat. Agents can work across code, merge requests, work items, and pipelines, and hand work to agentic flows within GitLab Duo Agent Platform. Each action runs under your existing GitLab permissions.

Built for how agents work

APIs are built for developers writing code. An agent that uses one has to work out which endpoints to call and make several calls to assemble one answer. Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard built for agents. An MCP server tells an agent what it can do and offers a curated set of tools designed around real workflows. Agents get the tools they need with more focused context, in fewer calls, and needing less data to carry through each task.

The GitLab MCP server applies that approach to your workflows across your projects, supporting all your team members within the GitLab permissions you already set.

Whether you're a developer handing a task to an agent or a team deciding how agents should work across your organization, your agents get tool coverage broad enough to complete the work, with access that follows each user’s GitLab permissions. Developers can even start GitLab Duo Agent Platform flows from the MCP-compatible coding agent they already use.

Here is Claude Code using the GitLab MCP server to start the Fix Pipeline flow in Duo Agent Platform:

More of your workflow, within reach of an agent

In addition to the tools announced in 19.4, the GitLab MCP server now includes more tools for working with code and pipelines, and for finding the right group or doc.

  • Code: add_branch starts a feature branch, get_repository_file reads a file at any ref, and semantic_search finds code by meaning, answering "where is this implemented?" without knowing the file or symbol name.
  • Pipelines: get_pipeline shows why a pipeline is red, with its jobs, downstream pipelines, and artifacts on request. list_pipelines surfaces patterns across recent runs, and get_artifact_file reads a single file from a job's artifacts, such as a log, report, or test fixture, without downloading the whole archive.
  • Orientation: list_groups lets an agent browse your group hierarchy to find the right group instead of guessing at identifiers, and list_wiki_pages, an opt-in tool, surfaces runbooks and docs before it answers a how-to question.

In 19.5, the MCP server tool catalog is also simpler to work with. Related tools are now consolidated, with fewer tools doing more. get_merge_request lets you ask your agent for a merge request’s commits, diffs, pipelines, conflicts, or notes. get_pipeline now includes get_pipeline_jobs, so you can ask for a pipeline’s jobs along with the pipeline itself. Your agents spend less time choosing the right tool and pull in only the details a task needs.

Toolsets let you choose which groups of tools the server returns. Each agent works from a focused set of tools that fits your team’s workflow instead of everything the server offers. A smaller set makes it less likely that an agent picks the wrong tool and has to retry. Most groups are on by default, and code security and wikis are available as opt-in groups. Browse the full catalog in the tools reference.

Start GitLab flows without leaving your client

Calling tools is one way an agent works with GitLab. Now, an agent can also hand a job to GitLab Duo Agent Platform and follow that job to the result without leaving your client. It can find the flows a project offers with list_duo_agents_and_flows, start a new flow from a goal in plain language with start_duo_session, and check progress with get_duo_session and list_duo_sessions. The work runs in a CI job inside GitLab, under the same context layer, policy checks, and audit trail as any other Duo Agent Platform session.

When a session needs a decision, it pauses for your input. With send_duo_session_input, you approve or reject the agent’s proposed action, or answer its question, and the session picks back up, keeping you in the loop. The duo_agent_platform toolset is included by default alongside the rest of the GitLab MCP server's tools.

Connect your agents to GitLab today

The agents supporting your software lifecycle will continue evolving. As your team adopts new agents, the GitLab MCP server connects each one to GitLab’s tools and flows, so they’re productive from day one.

You can connect the agents your team already uses by following the MCP server documentation, which includes setup instructions for Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, OpenAI Codex, Gemini, Kiro, Zed, and other MCP-compatible clients. The GitLab MCP server is available on the Free, Premium, and Ultimate tiers, on GitLab.com, GitLab Self-Managed, and GitLab Dedicated. On GitLab.com, per-user rate limits are set at 60 calls per minute on Free and 600 on Premium and Ultimate.

If you’re new to Duo Agent Platform, start a free trial. Already on Premium or Ultimate? Turn on Duo Agent Platform and use the GitLab Credits included with your subscription.

title: Unblock agentic software delivery with governed code review
summary:
AI agents have changed how much code a team can produce in a day. Review queues haven’t kept up, and delivery stalls while changes wait for a closer look. The usual workarounds (reminders, reviewer rotations, assigning a team) buy a little time and then burn people out.

Client-side review with AI helps the author by catching issues as the code is being written, before a merge request even opens. But it only goes so far. A review that only checks quality still leaves the organization without enforceable policy on the way to production, since comments on a diff do not decide whether a change can merge or reach production.

Every merge request still needs a consistent certification step tied to pipelines, security findings, code owners, approval rules, and audits. Review in the author’s environment cannot standardize that work across all your projects, route policy-bound changes to the right person, or show leaders what the agent did before the change merges. As agents write more of the code, automated reviews need to happen in the platform that already tracks each change from plan to production, and where identity, policy, and oversight controls are already in place.

Earlier this year, we made Code Review Flow generally available on GitLab Duo Agent Platform, bringing that sign-off to the merge request and making agentic review part of the same platform where code ships. Teams can turn it on so every change is automatically addressed under rules you set once, at $0.25 per review, delivering an estimated 100x ROI. That predictable unit cost is low enough to leave automatic review on for every merge request, which is how reviews move at machine speed while staying cost-efficient at organizational scale.

Agentic reviews, built for how you ship

Code Review Flow is native to GitLab merge requests, so it covers your whole environment. It runs as a CI/CD job on your runners, whether GitLab-hosted or your own, so review executes in the same environment as the rest of delivery. It works the same way on GitLab.com, GitLab Dedicated, and GitLab Self-Managed, keeping inference under your control with self-hosted models when air-gapped or regulated environments require it. You also have the flexibility to choose which model acts as the foundation for agentic code review: GitLab-managed or your own self-hosted models.

When certification is the default on the merge request, teams get coverage, control, and follow-through in one place. Here are the key highlights for agentic code review with GitLab Duo Agent Platform:

Every merge request is reviewed, without anyone having to ask. Turn on automatic reviews at the project, group, or instance level and settings cascade. Authors don’t have to remember to request a first pass.

Standards you set once for how the group ships. Custom review instructions capture language conventions, security practices, and path-specific rules. A group can point the Code Review Flow at a template project so those standards travel with the work. Pair guidance with GitLab’s enforced security and compliance controls when a requirement must always hold.

Follow-through on every finding. Follow-up review rechecks what GitLab Duo Agent Platform already flagged, verifies fixes, and avoids repeating the same points. At that price, you can leave automatic reviews everywhere.

The right human, when policy requires one. Code owners and relevant approval rules still apply. Recommend Reviewers Flow suggests the smallest group that can satisfy those rules based on their level of expertise, workload, availability, and timezone.

How agentic code review works in GitLab

Within GitLab, code review happens on the merge request, next to your pipelines, security findings, and approvals.

  1. A merge request opens (or becomes ready). Automatic review can start the Code Review Flow, or an author assigns GitLab Duo.
  2. The flow runs as a CI/CD job on your runners, analyzes the change with repository and merge request context, guided by your custom review instructions and the models your group selected, and comments on the diff.
  3. Authors and their coding agents push fixes. Follow-up review verifies Duo’s prior findings and carries context forward from the earlier pass.
  4. When a human must approve, Recommend Reviewers Flow proposes who should take the request; you assign from the merge request.
  5. Pipelines, security findings, approval rules, and the session record stay in the same place, so “reviewed” means certified on the path to production.

Deeper review when the change warrants it. An extended analysis pass will pull in calling code and tests for high-complexity merge requests, under your model-selection controls.

Clearer decisions on the merge request. GitLab Duo will be able to approve or request changes under settings you control.

Focus on risk. Risk assessment on the merge request will help teams see which changes deserve more attention.

Review before the merge request opens. Local review in Duo CLI will let developers run project review guidance against working-tree changes before the merge request runs the organization’s official check.

As agents write more of your code, you need reviewed code reaching production, with every change held to your standards and your reviewers focused on the changes that need a person. Every improvement on this roadmap is built to help you get there.

title: Gemini 4 Argon on GitLab: Built for long-running agentic work
summary:
As AI models take on longer, multi-step work, the challenge is putting that power to use across the software lifecycle without adding risk or cost. Teams need to be able to move faster, within enterprise controls and guardrails.

Google's Gemini 4 Argon, now available on GitLab Duo Agent Platform, was built for that kind of work. With Argon, your team can delegate long, multi-step actions and receive outputs for review. In GitLab's internal evaluation, Gemini 4 Argon completed 93.3% of GitLab’s software engineering benchmark tasks.

Reliable execution for long-horizon tasks

Work across the software lifecycle demands persistence and steady attention. Argon sustains its reasoning across the many steps of a task, reading files, running commands, and editing code through to completion. Your engineers can delegate to GitLab Duo agents powered by Argon with confidence and spend their time reviewing results instead of monitoring runs.

Google trained Argon to respect system boundaries, tell you when it couldn't find something or finish a task, and pause for confirmation before an irreversible step. Teams can hand off complex tasks and stay in control of the important decisions.

In internal evaluations, Argon resolved 73.3% of GitLab’s benchmark tasks, with each change passing the benchmark’s tests across multiple programming languages. Of the runs that hit a tool error or timeout, Argon still completed 93.8% of them, so a single failure mid-run won’t force your team to start over. Agent output lands in a merge request, where your team reviews the result with the full context of the change.

Argon works through problems thoroughly, making it a strong model choice when finishing correctly matters more than finishing fast.

Choose the Gemini model that fits your workload

Gemini 4 Argon is Google's newest frontier model and the most performant Gemini model on GitLab Duo Agent Platform. It handles long-horizon agentic actions especially well, including tasks that begin loosely defined. It pairs with the Flash models, which offer a lower-cost option for high-volume work, so you can match each workload to the best Gemini model. title: Scaling Git for the agentic software factory
summary:
AI agents are fundamentally changing the economics of software development. As the cost of producing code falls, the volume of changes moving through the software factory is accelerating beyond what infrastructure designed for human developers was built to handle.

GitLab anticipated this shift and began developing next-generation source code management (SCM) to support thousands of concurrent agents working against large repositories. In June, we announced next-gen SCM at GitLab Transcend, joined on stage by Nick G. from Anthropic's source control team. We've continued collaborating on the technical challenges of agent-scale development, and in August we shared more of our architecture and early performance results.

This week, Anthropic provided a compelling demonstration of why this work is so important. As daily merges to its monorepo grew from approximately 2,500 in May to more than 30,000 in September, its engineers built Scion, a specialized source control system designed for their environment.

Anthropic's experience reinforces the architectural direction we've been pursuing. Scion is purpose-built for enormous monorepos where nearly all clients are agents that are always online. Anthropic acknowledges that its approach isn't a general-purpose replacement for Git and requires its own code review, search, and CI infrastructure.

GitLab is building for the broader enterprise market: delivering agent-scale performance while preserving Git compatibility, infrastructure choice, and integration with the software development lifecycle.

"Scaling our monorepo for agentic development has changed how we think about Git server architecture. We see room to expand what Git servers can do for these workloads without departing from the overall Git model."

— Nick G., Source Control, Anthropic

Built on Git. Designed for agents.

Traditional Git workflows require clients to download substantial repository data, even when an agent needs only a small portion. A single agent invocation can involve 5–10 GB of data transfer and more than 30 seconds of setup, just to answer one question. Multiply that overhead across thousands of agents and source control becomes a bottleneck.

Most enterprises can't move source control onto new infrastructure just to scale it. Next-gen SCM preserves the Git protocol while modernizing the architecture underneath. Stateless compute scales horizontally against shared object storage, while agent-native interfaces let agents request the files and history they need without repeatedly cloning entire repositories.

In early internal tests, workloads completed up to 50x faster, used up to 2x fewer tokens, and generated up to 1,000x less network traffic compared with conventional workflows. These are peak improvements under specific test conditions, and we're continuing to validate performance under sustained, concurrent load.

The same architecture is designed to run on GitLab.com and on S3-compatible storage that customers control, including in air-gapped data centers. Repository data stays within the customer's infrastructure, preserving data sovereignty and existing investments while delivering the scalability agentic development demands.

For a closer look at the architecture and what we're building, watch Mark and Kranthi's latest next-gen SCM update:

Source control is only the first bottleneck

Speeding up source control alone moves the bottleneck downstream. An agent that writes code in seconds creates little value if the resulting changes spend hours waiting for validation, security review, or deployment.

Traditional merge queues and CI workflows face growing pressure when agents generate changes faster than validation can complete. We're seeing this pressure across GitLab.com. Over the past year, customers created 40% more CI/CD pipelines, while code pushes increased 50%. Agent-scale CI will need to validate more changes with less compute per change while preserving evidence of what was tested and verified.

This is why next-gen SCM is part of GitLab's broader vision for a governed software factory. As agents accelerate software production, source control, context, orchestration, CI, security, and governance must evolve together.

We're designing next-gen SCM to let thousands of agents work in parallel in isolated sessions, where unsuccessful experiments can be discarded without disrupting shared code. Successful changes can flow into GitLab's existing merge requests, pipelines, security checks, and governance controls on their path to production.

GitLab Orbit is being developed to provide a context graph of the entire software lifecycle, while GitLab Duo Agent Platform orchestrates agent work across stages. We're also advancing capabilities to make agents accountable for their work, including attribution and authorization of agent actions, preserving the instructions and decisions behind code changes, and giving reviewers the context needed to focus human judgment where it matters.

The goal is to reduce the time and total cost of moving software from intent to production, even as the number of agents and changes grows dramatically.

We believe a governed software factory offers the best economics for agentic development: more software delivered at lower cost per change, with the security and control enterprises require.

Advancing Git through open collaboration

Git's open ecosystem has been foundational to modern software development, and we believe it will remain essential in the agentic era. GitLab has long been an active contributor to Git, and we'll continue working with the community to advance the standard that millions of developers and tools depend on.

Our next-gen SCM architecture builds on that foundation, combining Git compatibility with a redesigned backend and agent-native interfaces designed to deliver the performance and scalability these new workloads demand.

This approach preserves the investments customers have made in Git while allowing GitLab to innovate rapidly across the broader software lifecycle. Our differentiation is the governed software factory: bringing source control, context, orchestration, security, and governance together on one platform.

What's next

Next-gen SCM is in private beta, and we're working with customers to validate performance against their own repositories and workloads.

As agents dramatically increase software production, the entire software factory must operate at machine scale. GitLab is building that foundation.

title: Make every AI credit count: See, cap, and reduce agent spend
summary:
Costs multiply with every task you hand to an agent. Each task consumes tokens and credits, and as agents spread across your teams and automations, consumption can grow faster than usage. title: GitLab's agent orchestration eliminates the wait between development stages
summary:
AI coding tools have changed how fast software gets written, but not how fast it ships. As code generation accelerates, the bottleneck moves downstream into verify, review, and ship. Those stages still run on human time. While agents write fixes in minutes, delivery slows on constant wait times and manual handoffs. Reviewer signoffs, pipeline alerts, scan triage, and step-by-step prompting are examples of obstacles DevOps teams face in maintaining on-time delivery.

At GitLab Transcend, we announced new agent orchestration capabilities in GitLab Duo Agent Platform to eliminate that delay. Goal-driven flows take the outcome you define and run it end to end, through review, tests, security scans, and approvals from Duo CLI, headless mode, or Agentic Chat. GitLab for Slack starts work from the conversation where it was requested, like turning a thread into an issue or kicking off a flow to fix a failing pipeline. Custom Flows let you define your own multi-step sequences and start them from GitLab events like a mention, an assignment, or a pipeline. All three run under your identity, policy, and evidence chain.

How agentic orchestration speeds up delivery

Faster coding, process checklists, and single-chat coding agents all contribute to delays in software delivery. With agentic orchestration capabilities, you can accelerate each stage and reclaim time for your development team.

Fewer handoffs. You name the goal, and the flow keeps working across review, tests, scans, and approvals instead of stopping between each step.

Start work where the request already is. A Slack thread becomes an issue or a flow immediately from where you’re already discussing the work.

Automate the process your team already follows. Custom Flows let you define your own multi-step sequences and start them from a mention, an assignment, or a pipeline.

Stay in control. Flows run under the same identity, policy, and evidence chain as the rest of GitLab, so governance stays with the work. Foundational agents and flows already cover plan through analyze stages in the GitLab UI, your IDE, and Duo CLI, and you can enable more from the AI Catalog, bring in external agents, and connect tools through the MCP client and the MCP server.

Goal-driven flows: Set your objective

Goal-driven flows give agents the finish line instead of the next step. You describe the objective and what done looks like, and the flow keeps working until it gets there. Goal-driven flows automate handoffs, so review, tests, security scans, and approvals run as one connected sequence.

You start one with the /goal command, for example:

/goal Fix the checkout timeout. Continue until tests pass and CI is green.

A separate model checks the work against your goal at each step, and you can stop or redirect a run at any point. You can start a goal-driven flow in Duo CLI, in headless mode with duo run --goal, and in Agentic Chat.

GitLab for Slack: Start where the work gets discussed

GitLab for Slack lets you start work in GitLab without leaving Slack. Mention @GitLab in any channel or thread and describe what you need, such as "fix the failing pipeline," and a flow starts. Duo streams its progress back into the thread, so your team follows the work where the conversation is already happening. The flow runs under the same identity and policy as any other GitLab flow, so governance stays in GitLab. You can also use @GitLab to ask questions about your codebase or create an issue from the conversation.

Custom Flows: Turn your process into a flow

Custom Flows chain agents together to match the process your team already follows. You define a flow once, start it from GitLab events like a mention, an assignment, or a pipeline, and run it in CI/CD pipelines. A self-healing pipeline, for example, can analyze a failed test, generate a fix, commit it, and notify your team, with human-in-the-loop checkpoints at sensitive steps. Each flow runs under the same identity, policy, and evidence chain as every other flow, so governance stays in GitLab.

Put agent orchestration to work

To achieve the benefits of agent orchestration, start with goal-driven flows. The documentation for Duo CLI slash commands walks you through /goal. Goal-driven flows are available on GitLab.com, GitLab Self-Managed, and GitLab Dedicated, on the Premium and Ultimate tiers, and require GitLab 19.3 or later and Duo CLI 9.17.0 or later.

Then extend that orchestration to your team's processes and channels with Custom Flows, which are generally available, and the MCP server and GitLab for Slack, which will be generally available later this month.

To design the foundation for your software factory, check out GitLab Duo Agent Platform. New to GitLab? Start a free trial of GitLab Duo Agent Platform. Already on Premium or Ultimate? Turn on GitLab Duo Agent Platform and use the GitLab Credits included with your subscription.

title: Track organization-wide security risk in one dashboard
summary:
If you run application security across more than one top-level group, getting a single organization-wide view of your risk has meant manually pulling together data. That is operational work rebuilt in spreadsheets and one-off scripts every time someone asks. This manual work is easy to get wrong, and is often out of date the moment it is published. Every hour spent assembling that view is an hour your security team is not spending on strategic work to drive down risk.

With GitLab 19.4, the security dashboard now gives you a consolidated view of risk at the organization level. Across every top-level group and every scanner your teams run, you can see how your whole application security program is doing, find where the real risk is concentrated, and act on it, without stitching anything together by hand. Your team spends its time remediating vulnerabilities instead of assembling reports, and when leadership or an auditor asks where the organization stands, you have a current, defensible answer on one screen. The organizational level security dashboard is available in beta for GitLab.com users.

See total risk, then triage down to the project

The risk score quantifies the risk level across the entire organization. This score is calculated based on the severity and age of your open vulnerabilities, whether each one appears on the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) list, and its Exploit Prediction Scoring System (EPSS) score. The risk score helps security leaders prioritize what area of the organization is most susceptible to threats, rather than a raw count that treats every finding as equal.

The charts around the risk score also proactively answer follow-up questions. The Vulnerabilities over time view shows whether risk is trending up or down across the organization over 30, 60, or 90 days. Vulnerabilities by age shows what is going stale and slipping past your remediation targets. Open vulnerabilities by severity and the top 10 Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) show the shape of the risk, so a weakness that recurs across the whole organization gets interpreted as a training or policy gap rather than a series of bugs. Filter the entire dashboard by project or by report type to focus on static application security testing (SAST) or dependency scanning vulnerability types.

Consolidate every scanner into one view

The organization dashboard isn’t limited to GitLab's own scanners. Any third-party scanner that outputs Static Analysis Results Interchange Format (SARIF) reports can feed its findings into GitLab. These become vulnerability records like any native finding and roll up into the same risk score, charts, and per-project view. For a security team running multiple tools across the organization, you get one consolidated read on risk, including GitLab's scanners and those you already run, rather than a separate dashboard per tool and manual efforts to combine them.

Turn on the organization security dashboard

The organization security dashboard is available in beta on GitLab.com for Ultimate. It reads the data your projects already produce, so switching it on depends on having the right pieces in place.

Before the dashboard can display your org-level risk, confirm four things:

  • You have created an Organization with multiple top-level groups using the Organizations (Beta) feature. To do this, Owners can Create Organizations under Settings > General > Advanced.
  • You have Owner role access to the Organization-level in GitLab.
  • Advanced search and advanced vulnerability management are active. These power the rollup across top-level groups, and on GitLab.com they are on by default.
  • Your projects run at least one security scanner and have a completed scan on their default branch, so there are vulnerabilities to aggregate.

With that in place, go to the top bar, select Search or Go to, and choose your Organization. In the left sidebar, select Secure, then Security dashboard. The organization view opens with the risk score and the charts across every top-level group in the organization.

Not on GitLab Ultimate yet? Start a free trial today to get organization-level visibility into your risk posture.

title: Dependency Firewall: Block risky packages before the build
summary:
Attackers disguise malicious packages as ones you trust. In June 2026, GitLab researchers found five malicious PyPI packages, four of them typosquats of Flask, Requests, and NumPy, that run at install time and steal CI/CD credentials. Additionally, AI coding agents now add open source dependencies on their own, often unreviewed, so developers don't have oversight into what packages may contaminate your build.

Once a malicious or vulnerable package enters your build, its code may run with the same access in your CI pipeline, and it can then reach any system your pipelines touch.

GitLab Dependency Firewall, introduced today at Transcend in early access, can block packages that match your policy, including malicious, vulnerable, and non-compliant packages, before they reach your build. Built-in governance stops risk before install, so your team doesn’t have to trace, remove, or rebuild what a policy blocks. Developers and their agents can keep pulling the dependencies they need without waiting on a manual security review, and packages that satisfy your policy requirements become part of your official build.

Watch the replay of our Transcend event to see demos of new platform capabilities and explore what it takes to carry the speed of agentic AI across the full software lifecycle.

Block malicious packages without breaking your build

Without a policy at the point of install, a bad package goes into the build first and gets caught later. Software composition analysis (SCA) scans what you've already pulled in, so by the time it flags a malicious package, a high-severity vulnerability, or a license your legal team won't accept, the dependency is installed and may have shipped in an artifact. Tracing where it went, pulling it out, and rebuilding turns a routine pipeline run into unplanned work for your engineering team.

With Dependency Firewall, you decide what's allowed into your builds before it's installed, by defining policies for:

  1. Malicious status — packages flagged in GitLab's malware advisory database
  2. Vulnerability severity — the severity you set (critical, high, medium, or low) and the number of findings you allow at that level, including zero
  3. License type — the licenses you allow or deny, listed by full name, and how to handle packages whose license can't be determined
  4. Package age — the minimum age a package must reach before it can enter a build, so a version published minutes ago can't go straight in before anyone has vetted it

Rolling out enforcement does not have to put delivery at risk. Start in warn mode, where the firewall records what a policy would catch, but lets the build continue. It leaves an audit event, a dashboard entry, and a line in the CI summary, so you can analyze whether or not to block the build.

Once you trust the policies, switch to block mode, which stops the pipeline on a match and gives the reason. When someone has a real need to get an approved package through, a logged bypass lets a designated user or token proceed, on the record.

Set policy once, or tailor it by team

A firewall that enforces only at the registry gives everyone the same policy, but that rarely fits how teams actually work. A payments service and an internal prototype carry very different risk, and your policy should treat them differently.

With Dependency Firewall, you set one policy at the top-level group and every project beneath it inherits the same rules. When a team needs something different, you can set a policy for that group or project.

You can also enforce policy at the registry, so every pull is checked, not just pulls from a pipeline. Rules live as code in a security policy project, so they are reviewed and changed through a merge request like the rest of your configuration. They inherit from the top-level group down to each project, and where rules overlap the strictest one applies. A critical service can be held above the organization's baseline, and no project drops below it.

Check a package before you pull it in

A developer, or an agent working on their behalf, usually finds out a package is not allowed only when the pipeline fails. That costs a build cycle and breaks concentration, right when the work is moving.

You get the answer from GitLab Dependency Firewall before you add a dependency, in the place you already work, allowing you to pick a package that passes the first time.

Using GitLab CLI within the terminal or within a script, a command line check can identify if a package will pass or be blocked by your policy, without requiring developers to open a separate console. It covers common package managers such as npm, pip, Poetry, Maven, Gradle, and Bundler, with more coming soon.

See and prove every decision

A security leader has to be able to prove what a control is doing during an audit. A control that blocks quietly, with no record, does not answer the auditor’s question and does not build trust with the teams it governs.

You get one view of what the firewall has allowed, warned against, and blocked, with an immutable record of each decision you can hand to an auditor.

A Dependency Firewall dashboard shows activity and outcomes across the projects in scope. Every warn, block, and bypass writes an audit event that records the rule that matched, the policy behind it, and the package involved.

Get early access to GitLab Dependency Firewall

You can stop malicious, vulnerable, and non-compliant packages before they reach a build. It is compatible with GitLab Artifact Central and external registries from Sonatype Nexus Repository and JFrog Artifactory, and does not require standing up a separate tool next to your GitLab deployment. Dependency Firewall is now in early access for GitLab.com and GitLab Self-Managed customers in the Premium or Ultimate tier. Request early access today!

title: Every artifact your teams ship, assembled right the first time
summary:
Every software build is assembled from open source packages, base images, and libraries, with your code on top. When one of those components is missing or has drifted, the build fails. At agent speed, those failures multiply, and no team can clear them as manual exceptions.

Project-by-project registry sprawl makes it worse because retention rules, storage limits, and publish access all live separately inside each project. Project-level design works when a person sets up each registry by hand, but breaks down when agents are running continuously across hundreds of projects.

At GitLab Transcend today, we announced GitLab Artifact Central: one organization-level registry that replaces hundreds of project-level ones, so every pull or publish by a human or an agent runs through the same governed door, enabling platform teams to assemble the right software the first time.

Here is more on why we developed Artifact Central, and how it can help your team.

Set policy once, enforce everywhere

In GitLab, retention rules, storage limits, and who can publish all live inside each project’s free package and container registry, configured on its own. GitLab Artifact Central moves that job up one level. Teams assign retention rules, quota settings, and access policies once at the organization level, instead of recreating them in every project underneath it.

Every repository is closed by default: Being a member of the organization is the gate, not the grant. Organization membership alone doesn't unlock a single repository until a role grants it. We’ve built four roles specifically for artifacts: Admin, Manager, Contributor, and Viewer. These roles are kept separate from GitLab's existing project roles, so granting someone access to a repository never touches their privileges anywhere else.

One URL for publishing, proxying, or both

Instead of navigating an internal wiki page explaining what is where, developers point to one URL for everything. GitLab Artifact Central does this through three repository types:

  • Hosted — The private packages and images your teams build and publish.
  • Remote — A proxy in front of an external source, like Docker Hub or Maven Central, with the connection tested before anything depends on it.
  • Virtual — A single endpoint that brings hosted and remote repositories together. GitLab checks the hosted repository first, then falls back to the remote source. The first external pull is cached, so subsequent pulls come directly from GitLab without another trip to the internet.

Virtual repositories matter most for teams comparing GitLab with other artifact management solutions. They give developers the familiar single-endpoint experience without requiring them to think about where an artifact lives. Whether it was built internally or pulled from an external registry, developers request it the same way. During the beta period, Artifact Central supports Maven, npm, Docker, and OCI, with more formats to follow.

Trace anything back, automatically

Here's the part that's hard to replicate outside GitLab. Every artifact that publishes through GitLab Artifact Central carries its build provenance automatically: which pipeline built it, which branch and commit it came from, who triggered the job. Since it is the same platform that ran the build, the registry already knows.

Authentication works the same way. Publishing and pulling use CI_JOB_TOKEN, the identity your pipelines already have, for people and agents alike. An agent publishing or pulling through CI pipelines uses that exact same job token, not a bolted-on service account with separate permissions to maintain. With a standalone registry, tracing an artifact back to its source means separately correlating IDs across your CI system and your registry – using a script someone owns and maintains. With Artifact Central, the pipeline, branch, commit, and job are already attached to the artifact itself.

Answer 'what did we publish?' in seconds

Artifact Central lives in the same platform as your code, merge requests, and pipelines, so artifacts published from CI carry their build provenance: the pipeline that built them, the commit, and who published them.

Next, we plan to connect that across your organization through GitLab Orbit, so "which of my running services are affected by this vulnerability?" becomes one question with one answer, instead of a manual search across four or five tools.

Pair Artifact Central with Dependency Firewall

GitLab Dependency Firewall, a separate GitLab product now in early access for Premium and Ultimate customers, works out of the box with Artifact Central. With Dependency Firewall, you can stop risky packages before they ever reach a build. You add its check to each pipeline using the glab CLI, so coverage is pipeline by pipeline, no matter which package manager your teams use. Next, we plan to enable tighter integration between the two capabilities, so that one policy for your whole organization blocks risky packages by vulnerability, license, or package age the moment they're pulled.

Two benefits of the same registry

Here's what that looks like from two different desks: a developer shipping code, and the platform team making sure the whole thing holds together.

A developer publishing from CI. Your pipeline publishes a Maven artifact using the job token it already has without any new secrets to manage. If that same developer needs an internal package alongside something from Maven Central, they point at one virtual repo URL and let GitLab Artifact Central sort out where each one actually lives.

A platform team setting policy once. Instead of configuring rules across 100s of separate projects, an admin sets storage quotas and repository access rules at the organization level, one time — and every repository underneath inherits it. When someone asks how much the company is storing, and where, there's one dashboard with the answer.

Migrating your artifacts

Most companies aren't starting from zero, and switching cold from an existing registry isn't realistic. With GitLab Artifact Central, you can add your existing repos as remotes behind a virtual repo, so developers point at one URL and artifacts move over only when a build actually asks for one. There is no need for bulk copies, weekend migration windows, or moving petabytes of data across your network.

Your old registry remains the system of record. When you're ready, you convert that remote to a hosted repo on Artifact Central. Your migration is safer and gradual.

Try Artifact Central, free in beta

GitLab Artifact Central is available today in beta for GitLab.com, with availability on GitLab Self-Managed planned for later this month. There's no billing during the beta, and nothing to purchase. We're tracking usage to shape pricing ahead of general availability, and we'll share details then.

Help us continue to build GitLab Artifact Central

None of this would be where it is without our design partners, who've been running Artifact Central with real workflows for weeks. Their feedback already shaped what's shipping today, and your feedback will shape what comes next.

No invitation is required to participate in the beta of Artifact Central, just sign up on our website and a member of our team will be in touch to help enable it for your account. If you don’t have a GitLab account yet, you can also sign up for the beta, and a member of our team will reach out.

We can't wait to see what you build.

Whether it was built internally or pulled from an external registry, developers request it the same way. During the beta period, Artifact Central supports Maven, npm, Docker, and OCI, with more formats to follow.

Trace anything back, automatically

Here's the part that's hard to replicate outside GitLab. Every artifact that publishes through GitLab Artifact Central carries its build provenance automatically: which pipeline built it, which branch and commit it came from, who triggered the job. Since it is the same platform that ran the build, the registry already knows.

Authentication works the same way. Publishing and pulling use CI_JOB_TOKEN, the identity your pipelines already have, for people and agents alike. An agent publishing or pulling through CI pipelines uses that exact same job token, not a bolted-on service account with separate permissions to maintain. With a standalone registry, tracing an artifact back to its source means separately correlating IDs across your CI system and your registry – using a script someone owns and maintains. With Artifact Central, the pipeline, branch, commit, and job are already attached to the artifact itself.

Answer 'what did we publish?' in seconds

Artifact Central lives in the same platform as your code, merge requests, and pipelines, so artifacts published from CI carry their build provenance: the pipeline that built them, the commit, and who published them.

Next, we plan to connect that across your organization through GitLab Orbit, so "which of my running services are affected by this vulnerability?" becomes one question with one answer, instead of a manual search across four or five tools.

Pair Artifact Central with Dependency Firewall

GitLab Dependency Firewall, a separate GitLab product now in early access for Premium and Ultimate customers, works out of the box with Artifact Central. With Dependency Firewall, you can stop risky packages before they ever reach a build. You add its check to each pipeline using the glab CLI, so coverage is pipeline by pipeline, no matter which package manager your teams use. Next, we plan to enable tighter integration between the two capabilities, so that one policy for your whole organization blocks risky packages by vulnerability, license, or package age the moment they're pulled.

Two benefits of the same registry

Here's what that looks like from two different desks: a developer shipping code, and the platform team making sure the whole thing holds together.

A developer publishing from CI. Your pipeline publishes a Maven artifact using the job token it already has without any new secrets to manage. If that same developer needs an internal package alongside something from Maven Central, they point at one virtual repo URL and let GitLab Artifact Central sort out where each one actually lives.

A platform team setting policy once. Instead of configuring rules across 100s of separate projects, an admin sets storage quotas and repository access rules at the organization level, one time — and every repository underneath inherits it. When someone asks how much the company is storing, and where, there's one dashboard with the answer.

Migrating your artifacts

Most companies aren't starting from zero, and switching cold from an existing registry isn't realistic. With GitLab Artifact Central, you can add your existing repos as remotes behind a virtual repo, so developers point at one URL and artifacts move over only when a build actually asks for one. There is no need for bulk copies, weekend migration windows, or moving petabytes of data across your network.

Your old registry remains the system of record. When you're ready, you convert that remote to a hosted repo on Artifact Central. Your migration is safer and gradual.

Try Artifact Central, free in beta

GitLab Artifact Central is available today in beta for GitLab.com, with availability on GitLab Self-Managed planned for later this month. There's no billing during the beta, and nothing to purchase. We're tracking usage to shape pricing ahead of general availability, and we'll share details then.

Help us continue to build GitLab Artifact Central

None of this would be where it is without our design partners, who've been running Artifact Central with real workflows for weeks. Their feedback already shaped what's shipping today, and your feedback will shape what comes next.

No invitation is required to participate in the beta of Artifact Central, just sign up on our website and a member of our team will be in touch to help enable it for your account. If you don’t have a GitLab account yet, you can also sign up for the beta, and a member of our team will reach out.

We can't wait to see what you build.

Watch the replay of our Transcend event to see demos of new platform capabilities and explore what it takes to carry the speed of agentic AI across the full software lifecycle.

title: Two front doors: Module-level access in a Django GRC app
summary:
GitLab's engineering team builds a lot of our own internal tooling, but one platform in particular forced us to rethink how we handle authorization: our internal GRC tool that serves two very different customer bases under one roof — our Security Compliance team and our Internal Audit team.

If you're building or maintaining an internal Django tool that's starting to serve more than one audience — different teams, different data classification levels, different data that shouldn't cross streams — this post walks through the problem we hit, how we solved it, and how you can apply the same pattern to your own app.

The challenge

Our original tool was a single Django app built for the Security Compliance team with login_required on every view. This was the correct approach until Internal Audit found a new use case for our tool that would include a completely separate workflow, with its own data, its own models, and its own sensitive information that Security Compliance should not see.

login_required answers exactly one question: Are you logged in? It doesn't answer the question that actually matters in a multi-tenant internal tool: Are you allowed to be here? An authenticated Security Compliance user hitting an Internal Audit URL waltzed right past the login check and into data they were never supposed to see.

If your app has ever grown a second audience after the fact, this probably sounds familiar. The question worth asking yourself right now is simple: Does every view in your app check who the user is, or just whether they're logged in? If it's the latter, you likely have the same gap we did.

We needed clean separation — not "pay no attention to this button over here," but an enforced boundary that holds regardless of what URL someone types in.

The architectural decision

When Internal Audit's use case landed on our roadmap, we had the classic fork in the road: Bolt it onto the existing app or restructure? We restructured.

The result is a core Django project — shared auth, user management, audit logging, base UI components — with two independent module apps sitting on top of it. One is for Security Compliance and one is for Internal Audit. Each module owns its own models, views, and API surface.

The constraint we imposed on ourselves, and the one that made this whole thing worth writing about was that core has zero knowledge of compliance or internal audit data. Either module can depend on core. Neither module should depend on the other. That constraint keeps this from becoming two apps stitched together with duct tape and super glue.

Access control

We're a compliance engineering subdivision building a tool that stores sensitive compliance and risk data. Sloppy access control here isn't just a bug, it's a serious credibility problem.

Our design decision was to use something already native to Django: the built-in auth system. Each module maps to exactly one group. A user can belong to one group, both, or neither, and the system enforces the right separation of duty at every layer regardless of which combination applies. The navigation UI, the Django views, and the REST API each independently enforce group membership.

The implementation

There is one reusable class in core that both modules inherit from: GroupRequiredMixin. It checks group membership and raises PermissionDenied if the user isn't in the required group.

Module-level subclasses

Each module gets a three-line subclass that sets required_group_name — a GasGroupRequiredMixin and an IsGasGroupMember for the Security Compliance side, with the same pattern repeating for Internal Audit. That's the whole cost of adding a module's enforcement layer: one new file, one new attribute. The actual checking logic lives in core and never gets touched again.

The UI layer

Finally, there is a template filter, user_in_group, so navigation only renders what a user is actually allowed to view. It wraps a check like user|user_in_group:'erm' around any nav block that should only show up for ERM members.

This is a UX guard, not a security boundary. Hiding a navigation link doesn't stop anyone from typing the URL directly. That's what the mixins and the Django REST Framework permission class are for. The template filter just keeps the UI honest about what a given user can see and do.

What's next for us - and where you could start

Step back out to the platform level and the payoff is that this is a repeatable pattern that is module- and team-agnostic. A hypothetical third module — a vendor risk workflow, an audit management module, whatever comes next — inherits the same access control structure, the same audit trail, and the same shared authentication without a single new line of enforcement logic. The cost of a new module becomes almost entirely a business requirement, not infrastructure scaffolding.

That's the bet we made: Build the foundation once and let every future module ride on top of it instead of reinventing access control from scratch.

If you want to try this in your own app, here's roughly the order we'd suggest:

  1. Check your views for the login-versus-authorization gap. Grep for login_required and LoginRequiredMixin and ask, for each one, whether it's actually guarding sensitive data from other authenticated users — not just anonymous ones.
  2. Draw the module boundary before you write code. Decide what's genuinely shared (auth, base UI, logging) versus what belongs to one audience only.
  3. Write one mixin, not one per view. A single GroupRequiredMixin in your core app, subclassed per module, means your enforcement logic has exactly one place to be reviewed and one place to be wrong.
  4. Enforce at every layer independently — views, API, and navigation — so hiding a link is never your only line of defense.

References

  • Django class-based views — Using UserPassesTestMixin / permission mixins
  • Django REST Framework — Permissions
